newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian police say Kalimantan safe after riots.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian police say Kalimantan safe after riots.

text.p: Calm returned to Indonesia's West Kalimantan province on Saturday following fresh ethnic clashes, police and residents said, but the extent of casualties from the violence was unclear.
"Tebas is safe and under control," said one policeman, referring to the village where local Dayak tribesman clashed with migrants from the Indonesian island of Madura on Friday.

The policeman said Tebas, about 150 km (93 miles) north of the provincial capital of Pontianak, had "a social problem" on Friday but he declined to elaborate. When asked about injuries or deaths the policeman said: "I cannot give an explanation about that." The telephone line was then cut.

Lieutenant-Colonel Sjachranuddin, spokesman for the regional military command covering the Indonesian half of Borneo island, was quoted in Saturday's Banjarmasin Post in neighbouring South Kalimantan as saying people had been hurt in Tebas.

"There (are) certainly victims, but we do not know the amount for certain. Maybe they are just light injuries (or) serious injuries...rather than deaths. We still do not know for sure about the victims," he was quoted as saying on Saturday.
Police on Friday had been unable to give details of the renewed ethnic violence or declined to comment.
Church sources in Sambas, 20 km (12 miles) north of Tebas, said they had heard two people had been killed in Friday's clash and a number of buildings burnt but details remained sketchy.
The indigenous Dayaks are often Christian and the Madurese Moslem in mostly Islamic Indonesia, where various ethnic and religious riots have left at least 12 people dead since October.
Residents in Pontianak said the provincial capital was calm on Saturday. The situation in the regional towns of Singkawang and Sanggau was not immediately known.
Soldiers have blocked key roads from Pontianak leading to the province's interior for the past week.
Marzuki Darusman, deputy chairman of the official National Commission on Human Rights, said the body was monitoring the situation but had not yet decided to send a team to the area.

"We are not denying that things are still developing there but we think it is for the authorities to take care of them," Darusman told Reuters, adding the commission usually acted if the government was slow in intervening.

The tension, which residents say began in late December, exploded on New Year's Day when about 5,000 Dayak tribesmen rioted in Sanggau Ledo, 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak, attacking the Madurese. At least five died in the clashes.

Residents in Sanggau, 140 km (87 miles) east of Pontianak, said five Dayaks were killed last week when a crowd of about 200 Dayaks attacked a camp of more than 1,000 Madurese refugees guarded by soldiers.
The Madurese had fled to the town after earlier fighting.
